subject: Brexit referendum poll analysis - using a hierarchical Bayesian model (no shrinkage unexpectedly!)

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Brexit referendum poll analysis - using a hierarchical Bayesian model (no shrinkage unexpectedly!)
parts:
Hello all,

I am analysing the latest 25 polls for the Brexit polls in the UK. The reason I am doing it is because I think it will make a nice hierarchical Bayesian model case study for a class I am teaching. 

In the various polls (carried out by a range of agencies) people were asked: 'In a referendum in Britain's membership in the EU how would you vote?' They were then given three categories: a. Remain, b. Leave and c. Don't know. (There are some polls where people were also given another category 'I prefer not to say', but I have lumped that with 'Don't know' for simplicity.)

The polls were all carried out over the last month or so, and there haven't been any trends in the polls over this period. This makes me think that the data is probably exchangeable, conditional on an overarching distribution representing the UK population's preferences. 

As such, I have fit a simple hierarchical model to the data where I do not include any covariates. This model is shown below. Hopefully it is all (fairly) self explanatory. However, I may be being a bit naive by saying that!

I also attach the data if anyone else wants to play with it (thought this might make a nice example somewhere.) K = 25 if you want to run the model below.

My question is the following - when I estimate the below model, it yields parameter estimates of theta which are basically indistinguishable from the non-hierarchical model where I estimate them all separately. I was expecting there to be (at least some) shrinkage to the grand mean. However, this does not appear to be the case.

Does anyone know why this might be? One thing that occurs is that the numbers in each poll are typically above 1000 people, and hence the data in each is 'big enough' and hence has lower enough variance, such that there isn't any shrinkage. However, I may be making a silly mistake somewhere that I haven't picked up!

Best,

Ben

data {
  int<lower=1> K; ## Number of polls = 25
  int<lower=0> Y[K,3]; ## Vector of numbers voting for remain, leave and don't know in each poll
  int<lower=0> N[K]; ## Vector of total poll numbers for each poll (the sum of each row of Y)
}

parameters {
  simplex[3] theta[K]; ## Voter preferences in each poll
  vector<lower=0>[3] alpha; ## Overarching hierarchical distribution
} 
model {
  for (i in 1:K){
          Y[i] ~ multinomial(theta[i]);
          theta[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
          for (j in 1:3){
            if (j < 3){
                alpha[j] ~ gamma(3,1); ## Give a higher prior weight to the remain and leave categories than don't know
            } else{
            
                alpha[j] ~ gamma(1,1);
            }
            
          } 
  }
}

generated quantities{
    int<lower=0> YSim[K,3]; ## Data simulated assuming that we know the poll
    int<lower=0> YSimAnon[K,3]; ## Data simulated assuming that we are doing 25 new polls of unknown origin
    simplex[3] aTheta;
    
   for (i in 1:K){
       YSim[i] <- multinomial_rng(theta[i],N[i]);
       aTheta <- dirichlet_rng(alpha);
       YSimAnon[i] <- multinomial_rng(aTheta,N[i]);
   }
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Brexit referendum poll analysis - using a hierarchical Bayesian model (no shrinkage unexpectedly!)
parts:
There's a bug in your model. You don't want to provide
the prior K times in the loop, so the prior is really propto
a big product of gammas.

I think what you want instead of

for (i in 1:K){
Y[i] ~ multinomial(theta[i]);
theta[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
for (j in 1:3){
if (j < 3)
alpha[j] ~ gamma(3,1);

} else{
alpha[j] ~ gamma(1,1);
}
}

is

theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
alpha[1:2] ~ gamma(3, 1);
alpha[3] ~ gamma(1, 1);
for (k in 1:K)
Y[k] ~ multinomial(theta[k]);

Your model's pretty close to a Dirichlet-multinomial generalization
of the beta-binomial example I gave in the case study on pooling,
which covers the issue of how much pooling is going on and how it works.

I'd recommend an alternative and more easily formulated prior
for Dirichlet, removing the alpha parameters and adding kappa
and phi:


parameters {
real<lower = 1> kappa;
simplex[3] phi;

adding data to specify the prior for phi:

data {
vector<lower=0>[3] beta; // beta = prior counts for outcomes

and then in the model, using:

phi ~ dirichlet(beta);
kappa ~ pareto(1, 1.5);
theta ~ dirichlet(kappa * phi);

It's just much easier to interpret this way as independently putting
a prior on the population mean (theta) and prior count (kappa - 2). The
count is how you weight the prior with the actual observations.

If the counts in the polls are much higher than kappa, then the estimates
will come out near the ML estimates.

- Bob

parts:
Hi all,

So I have changed the model (I think as Bob wanted, but do correct me if wrong) to the below. However I am still seeing the same thing - when I look at the estimates from the heterogeneous model, they are very close to those from the hierarchical one. They're not exactly the same, but the amount of shrinkage is basically nothing. If my model's not wrong I would say this is due to the amount of data in each poll, and perhaps not using the correct likelihood. I think as Bob mentioned it would be better to use a Dirichlet-Multinomial likelihood to account for over-dispersion in the data.

What do people think?

Ben

data {
  int<lower=1> K; ## Number of polls

int<lower=0> Y[K,3]; ## Vector of numbers voting for remain, leave and don't know in each poll
  int<lower=0> N[K]; ## Vector of total poll numbers for each poll (the sum of each row of Y)

vector<lower=0>[3] beta;  // beta = prior counts for outcomes 
}

parameters {
  simplex[3] theta[K]; ## Voter preferences in each poll
simplex[3] phi; ## Overarching hierarchical distribution

real<lower = 1> kappa; 
}
model {

phi ~ dirichlet(beta); 
  kappa ~ pareto(1, 1.5);
for (i in 1:K){
theta[i] ~ dirichlet(kappa * phi);

Y[i] ~ multinomial(theta[i]);
  }
}

generated quantities{
    int<lower=0> YSim[K,3]; ## Data simulated assuming that we know the poll
    int<lower=0> YSimAnon[K,3]; ## Data simulated assuming that we are doing 25 new polls of unknown origin
    simplex[3] aTheta;
    
   for (i in 1:K){
       YSim[i] <- multinomial_rng(theta[i],N[i]);
aTheta <- dirichlet_rng(kappa * phi);

YSimAnon[i] <- multinomial_rng(aTheta,N[i]);
   }
}

Now the heterogeneous model (just using flat priors here, implicitly.)

data {
  int<lower=1> K;
  int<lower=0> Y[K,3];
  int<lower=0> N[K];

}

parameters {
  simplex[3] theta[K];
}

model {
  for (i in 1:K){
          Y[i] ~ multinomial(theta[i]);
  }
}

generated quantities{
    int<lower=0> YSim[K,3];

for (i in 1:K){
       YSim[i] <- multinomial_rng(theta[i],N[i]);
   }
}

parts:
You caught the fact that Dirichlet isn't vectorized yet. We
need to do the rest of the multivariate ones.

prior weight: (kappa - 2)

likelihood weight: sum(Y[i])

It may just be that you have large enough counts in Y[i] that
the prior doesn't do much.

One way to understand this and other models is through simulation.
Simulate data according to the model and see if the posterior is
well calibrated to the data (the posterior p% intervals contain p%
of the parameter values).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Brexit referendum poll analysis - using a hierarchical Bayesian model (no shrinkage unexpectedly!)
parts:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for your reply.

I've been doing that - generated simulated data. It does seem that if there is enough variation in the data (i.e. in the percentages voting in each category) then there is limited/no shrinkage to the grand mean. Explicitly I generated fake data by simulating from the Dirichlet-Multinomial distribution in R, then fitted each of the models. When instead I used the 'vanilla' Multinomial to generate the data, I did see shrinkage, even using the sort of sample sizes that I am looking at.

When using the Multinomial likelihood to fit the data this results in overly precise estimates of the percentages of people voting for each category. (This is the same issue as fitting a binomial distribution when a beta-binomial is more appropriate.) I think if I did fit a Dirichlet-Multinomial model then I would see this shrinkage. What do you think?

I have had look in the Stan manual and can't seem to find this distribution (a Dirichlet-Multinomial). Is this correct? If so, I will code up the model in Mathematica and see how it fares.

Best,

Ben
